content: Rifaximin is an antibiotic used to treat diarrhea caused by Escherichia coli (commonly referred to as traveler's diarrhea). It is not effective for diarrhea accompanied by fever, bloody stools, or caused by pathogens other than E. coli. This medication is also used to manage irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea. It is important to note that rifaximin is only effective against bacterial infections and does not work for viral infections such as the common cold or flu. When taking rifaximin, it is essential to follow the prescribed dosage and complete the full course of treatment, even if symptoms improve after a few days. If diarrhea persists beyond 1 to 2 days, or if it is accompanied by fever or bloody stools, consult your doctor immediately. Rifaximin may interact with other medications, particularly those that are substrates of the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter. Co-administration with P-gp inhibitors can significantly increase systemic exposure to rifaximin, potentially leading to adverse effects. For example, combining rifaximin with cyclosporine has been shown to result in an 83-fold increase in peak plasma concentration (Cmax) and a 124-fold increase in area under the curve (AUC) in healthy individuals. Therefore, close monitoring and potential dose adjustments of P-gp substrates may be necessary when used concurrently with rifaximin. Patients with severe hepatic impairment should be monitored closely due to the potential for increased systemic exposure to rifaximin. Additionally, rifaximin may reduce the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine, and should be used with caution in such cases. Common side effects of rifaximin include flatulence (11%), headache (10%), rectal tenesmus (7%), abdominal pain (7%), urgency of defecation (6%), nausea (5%), constipation (4%), fever (3%), and vomiting (2%). Rare but serious adverse reactions include hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., allergic dermatitis, pruritus, rash), rhabdomyolysis in patients with cirrhosis, and severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). If symptoms worsen or persist for more than 24–48 hours, discontinue use and seek medical attention. Rifaximin is not effective against diarrhea caused by Campylobacter jejuni, Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, or traveler's diarrhea due to Shigella or Salmonella species. There is also a risk of pseudomembranous colitis, which should be considered in patients presenting with severe or prolonged diarrhea. During pregnancy, rifaximin should only be used if clearly needed, as its safety has not been fully established. It is unknown whether rifaximin passes into breast milk, so caution is advised for nursing mothers. Rifaximin is primarily excreted in feces (>90%) and has a half-life of 2–5 hours. It can be taken with or without food. Store the medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. In the U.S., call 911 or the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222. In Canada, contact your local poison control center. This medication has been prescribed for your current condition only. Do not use it for other conditions unless directed by your doctor. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
